summary: Specifies two encryption types and two checksum types for Kerberos 5, based on the Camellia block cipher in CBC mode with ciphertext stealing and the CMAC algorithm. It is informational and not an Internet Standards Track specification.

eli5.summary: Kerberos locks its messages with a secret code. This memo adds a new lock type, called Camellia, for Kerberos to use.

subtitle: New encryption and checksum types for Kerberos using the Camellia block cipher.

tldr.problem: Kerberos 5 relies on AES for encryption, but some organizations may need or prefer the Camellia block cipher for policy or regulatory reasons.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC specifies two encryption types (camellia128-cts-cmac and camellia256-cts-cmac) and two checksum types (cmac-camellia128 and cmac-camellia256) using the Camellia cipher in CBC mode with ciphertext stealing, key derivation via KDF-FEEDBACK-CMAC, and CMAC for integrity protection.
tldr.outcome: Kerberos implementations can now use Camellia encryption alongside AES, giving organizations additional cipher options while maintaining compatibility with the Kerberos framework.

today: RFC 6803 is published as Informational. It provides Kerberos implementations with standardized Camellia encryption and checksum types, registered with IANA under encryption type numbers 25-26 and checksum type numbers 17-18.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Camellia block cipher, defined in RFC 3713, is a 128-bit block cipher with support for 128-bit, 192-bit, or 256-bit keys. This RFC specifies how to use Camellia within the Kerberos cryptosystem framework (RFC 3961) for both encryption and checksum operations. Like AES encryption in Kerberos (RFC 3962), the new types use key derivation, CBC mode with ciphertext stealing to avoid padding, and PBKDF2 for key generation from passwords.

The two encryption types support 128-bit and 256-bit protocol keys, and the two corresponding checksum types use the CMAC algorithm (Cipher-based Message Authentication Code) for integrity protection. The new types do not follow the simplified Kerberos profile but instead use a more flexible key derivation function from NIST Special Publication 800-108.
sections.eli5: Kerberos is a system that lets computers prove they are who they say they are. It uses codes to scramble messages. This memo adds Camellia, a new scrambling method, as an option.

sections.title: Encryption Algorithm
sections.content:
The two encryption types are camellia128-cts-cmac (128-bit key) and camellia256-cts-cmac (256-bit key). Both use the same algorithm: encryption in CBC mode with ciphertext stealing (CTS) to handle messages that are not a multiple of the block size, and CMAC for integrity checking.

Encryption works by first generating a random 128-bit confounder, then using the encryption key (Ke) to encrypt the confounder and the plaintext in CBC-CTS mode. A message authentication code is computed over the confounder and plaintext using the integrity key (Ki) with CMAC. The final ciphertext is the encrypted data followed by the CMAC tag. Decryption reverses this: decrypt the ciphertext, verify the CMAC tag, and extract the plaintext.
sections.eli5: The message gets a random prefix added, then is scrambled with Camellia, then a checksum is added to detect tampering.

sections.title: Key Derivation and Generation
sections.content:
Three keys are derived from the base protocol key: Kc (for checksums), Ke (for encryption), and Ki (for integrity). These are derived using KDF-FEEDBACK-CMAC, a key derivation function from the NIST SP 800-108 family. The KDF uses CMAC with Camellia as the underlying function and a block counter in big-endian format.

When generating keys from passwords, the algorithm first prepends the encryption type name (camellia128-cts-cmac or camellia256-cts-cmac) to the salt string, then applies PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA1 with a default iteration count of 32,768. Finally, the result is passed through KDF-FEEDBACK-CMAC with the constant 'kerberos' to produce the final protocol key. This ensures that AES and Camellia keys are different even with the same password, preventing interoperability issues.
sections.eli5: The long-term secret key is processed through several functions to create three working keys: one for checking messages, one for scrambling, and one for protecting.

sections.title: Checksum Algorithm
sections.content:
The checksum types cmac-camellia128 and cmac-camellia256 use the CMAC algorithm (NIST SP 800-38B) with Camellia-128 or Camellia-256 as the block cipher. CMAC is a deterministic message authentication code that produces a 128-bit output for both key sizes. The checksum is computed by applying CMAC to the message using the checksum key (Kc).

Because CMAC is deterministic, an attacker could theoretically pre-compute checksums for known messages across many keys. However, this is a known trade-off of 128-bit checksums and applies to most Kerberos checksum types. Deployments can mitigate this by rotating keys frequently.
sections.eli5: A quick check number is calculated from the message using Camellia to catch any tampering.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC notes that CBC mode with 128-bit blocks can theoretically suffer from block collision attacks after observing 2^64 messages with the same key. This concern applies to all prior Kerberos encryption types and other protocols using CBC with 128-bit blocks. Mitigation is key rotation: by rolling over keys frequently enough that 2^64 messages are unlikely in a single key lifetime, the risk is reduced.

The deterministic nature of CMAC means that checking for pre-computed checksums across keys is theoretically possible, but this also applies to most standardized Kerberos checksum types. The RFC recommends deploying Camellia only if there is a business need for it or if a flaw is discovered in AES that does not affect Camellia. At the time of publication, no weak keys or security problems had been found in Camellia.
sections.eli5: If someone watches billions of messages with the same key, they might find patterns. Fixing this is easy: change the key every so often. Camellia itself is secure.
